paras: The killing of John Swancey was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Mark Crumpley, a man acting as a deputy, at Waverly, Missouri, on the night of the town's city election, Tuesday, April 7, 1903. The shooting came as officers tried to break up an election-night disturbance among Black residents in which the city marshal was beaten. A wire paragraph calling it an election riot started by 'blacks' ran in papers across the country, while Lafayette County papers added a self-defense claim and the visit of the sheriff and coroner.

Waverly held its city election on Tuesday, April 7, choosing a mayor, two aldermen, a marshal and a street commissioner. According to the wire report, two Black men from 'a negro settlement' at Waverly were among those running for alderman. The Lexington Intelligencer said instead that one Black candidate had been defeated and that Black residents were celebrating his defeat.

After the polls closed, City Marshal Wood McGrew tried to disperse a crowd of Black residents who, the Intelligencer said, were 'raising too much disturbance', and he was badly beaten. Constable A. H. Ledford then deputized Mark Crumpley to help end the trouble, and in what the Intelligencer called 'the attack on Crumpley' he shot and killed John Swancey. A Lexington dispatch of April 10 gave the officer's account: Swancy resisted arrest and assaulted Crumpley, who said he was compelled to shoot in self-defense.
The town's own correspondent described the shooter as 'Mack Crumpley a white man' and the dead man as 'Chas. Swanson, a colored man.'

The sheriff and the coroner went to Waverly after the shooting. No report of an inquest verdict, an arrest of Crumpley, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage, and no account from Black residents of Waverly was found.

The story reached most readers through a single Waverly wire paragraph dated April 8, which said that 'a number of blacks started a riot' and that Crumpley shot Swancey 'in trying to quell the disturbance.' The Santa Fe New Mexican ran it as 'Election Riots' on April 8, and the next day the Salt Lake Herald headed it 'Race Riot' while the Indianapolis Journal folded it into a column of telegraphic brevities. In Missouri, the St. Louis Republic headlined the same text 'Negroes Riotous at Waverly / One Darky Killed—City Marshal Severely Beaten.'

The Salt Lake Herald also used the killing for an editorial jab, asking, 'Can it be possible that negroes are allowed to vote in Missouri?' Closer to home, the Lexington Intelligencer gave the shooting a short front-page item, 'Negro Killed at Waverly,' and its Waverly correspondent mentioned it in a single line at the end of a column of social notes. Every surviving account came from white papers and rested on the officers' version; no coverage in the Black press was found.

The reports disagree on Crumpley's office: the wire called him a deputy sheriff, the Intelligencer said the constable deputized him on the spot, and the April 10 dispatch called him a constable. They also differ on the cause, from a riot over two Black candidates in the wire, to a celebration of one candidate's defeat in the Intelligencer, to resisting arrest in the constable's account. Three reports name the dead man John Swancey or Swancy, while the Waverly column alone calls him Chas. Swanson.

reader.title: Killing of John Swancey
bases: A man described as a deputy sheriff, a deputy, a constable, or a man deputized by the constable shot and killed a Black man while officers tried to end an election-night disturbance (A1, A9, A12).

The wire report (A1), the Lexington Intelligencer's county account (A9), its Waverly correspondent (A10) and a separate Lexington dispatch (A12) agree that Crumpley shot and killed Swancey at Waverly on election night, though they differ on names, Crumpley's office and the cause.

accounts.label: Wire report (Waverly, April 8)
accounts.gist: Blacks in a 'negro settlement' started a riot over two of their number running for alderman; deputy Mark Crumpley, trying to quell it, shot and killed John Swancey, and Marshal McGrew was badly beaten.

accounts.label: Lexington Intelligencer (county seat)
accounts.gist: After Tuesday's election Black residents were 'raising too much disturbance' celebrating the defeat of one of their number; McGrew was beaten trying to disperse them, Constable Ledford deputized Crumpley, and in the attack on Crumpley he shot Swancey.

accounts.label: Constable's claim (Lexington dispatch, April 10)
accounts.gist: Swancy resisted arrest and assaulted the constable, who says he was compelled to shoot in self-defense; the trouble arose from the defeat of Black candidates.

accounts.label: Waverly correspondent
accounts.gist: Notes only that 'Chas. Swanson, a colored man' was shot and killed by 'Mack Crumpley a white man' on the evening of the city election.

framing.detail: Papers from New Mexico to Indiana and Utah ran the Waverly wire paragraph blaming 'blacks' for starting a riot, under headings such as 'Election Riots' and 'Race Riot.'
The St. Louis Republic headlined 'Negroes Riotous at Waverly / One Darky Killed—City Marshal Severely Beaten.'
A Salt Lake Herald squib used the killing to ask sarcastically whether 'negroes are allowed to vote in Missouri.'
The Lexington papers' accounts rest on the officers' version: the disturbance, the beating of the marshal, and self-defense.

conflicts.note: Three reports, including the county-seat front page, give John Swancey; the Waverly social column alone gives Chas. Swanson.
